#3489. Catherine O'Hara's 8 Funniest Movie & TV Performances Ranked, Including Home Alone

Catherine O'Hara was one of the funniest people to ever grace entertainment. She has an amazing ability to make even the weirdest characters feel like real people. Whether she was giving a ridiculous line or showing a depth of emotion that you wouldn’t expect behind her wacky characters, she always knew how to create some incredible comedy with subtlety. Often her acting would be very detailed, and audiences could get as much enjoyment out of the smallest of facial expressions or change in tone as from the script itself.

Over the course of more than five decades, O'Hara has been involved in many different forms of comedy, including sketch, indie films, blockbusters and TV. She has worked with some of the most unique comedians and had some incredibly successful long-term partnerships with Eugene Levy and Christopher Guest. Theses led to some incredible mockumentaries where her improvisational skills could truly flourish.

O'Hara's greatest comedic achievement was arguably her fearlessness. She could play characters who were desperately self-important, spectacularly oblivious or completely detached from reality without losing the humanity that made them so enjoyable.

Christopher Guest's Hollywood satire For Your Consideration is a particularly entertaining exploration of the absurdity surrounding movie awards. O’Hara plays Marilyn Hack, an actress starring in the independent period drama Home for Purim, whose prospects suddenly change when rumors circulate that she might receive an Academy Award nomination.

O'Hara expertly conveys Marilyn's increasingly desperate relationship with celebrity. Her performance captures the way an ordinary person can become almost unrecognizable when surrounded by agents, publicity campaigns and the possibility of professional validation.

The funniest moments are often when O'Hara exposes Marilyn's insecurity without making her entirely unsympathetic. Her increasingly affected behavior and awkward attempts to navigate Hollywood's publicity machinery make for excellent satire, particularly alongside Eugene Levy's similarly recognition-hungry character.

It's a wonderfully observed performance, although Marilyn's comic predicament doesn't quite offer the same memorable character work as O'Hara's strongest collaborations with Guest.

Christopher Guest's A Mighty Wind is an affectionate mockumentary about a reunion concert celebrating several influential 1960s folk groups. O’Hara plays Mickey Crabbe, formerly one half of the successful musical duo Mitch & Mickey, alongside Eugene Levy's Mitch Cohen.

Their complicated history provides the film's emotional center. After considerable professional success together, their romantic relationship ended painfully, leaving Mitch with unresolved feelings that become increasingly apparent as they prepare for their reunion performance.

O'Hara is particularly funny when Mickey discusses her musical career with an almost entirely straight-faced seriousness, especially when recalling the duo's unusual experiences and the peculiar circumstances surrounding their separation.

The highlight is undoubtedly the Oscar-nominated song "A Kiss at the End of the Rainbow." O'Hara and Levy make the performance genuinely moving, allowing the characters' complicated feelings to emerge through their music. This emotional sincerity in A Mighty Wind is precisely what makes the comedy work so well.

O'Hara's years on SCTV established the foundations of her distinctive comedic style. It allowed her to experiment with impressions, exaggerated personalities and recurring characters over several years. Having joined Toronto's Second City before becoming part of the television ensemble, she developed an impressive collection of comic creations that demonstrated her extraordinary versatility.

Among her most memorable characters was Lola Heatherton, an aggressively cheerful lounge singer whose confidence dramatically exceeded her actual talent. O'Hara's exaggerated smiles, theatrical gestures and increasingly desperate attempts to maintain her glamorous image made Lola an exceptionally funny parody of entertainment personalities.

O'Hara tackled celebrity impressions including Brooke Shields, Lucille Ball, Meryl Streep and Katharine Hepburn, frequently finding hilarity in their speech patterns and public personas rather than relying on superficial physical resemblance.

Although her later film and television characters became more widely recognized, Second City Television was where O'Hara proved just how inventive her comedy could be.

O'Hara's first major collaboration with Christopher Guest remains one of her funniest. In Waiting for Guffman, O’Hara plays Sheila Albertson, a travel agent in the fictional Missouri town of Blaine who dreams of becoming a successful theatrical performer.

Married to Ron (Fred Willard), Sheila considers herself part of an exceptionally talented entertainment partnership, despite the couple's rather limited abilities. Their audition for the town's anniversary musical, featuring a hilariously awkward rendition of "Midnight at the Oasis," is an absolute masterclass in playing complete artistic incompetence with absolute sincerity.

O'Hara's comic timing is particularly effective during the couple's interactions. She frequently anticipates Ron's dialogue, enthusiastically joining in before he has finished speaking.

The Chinese restaurant scene is another standout. As Sheila becomes increasingly intoxicated, O'Hara gradually shifts her delivery and physical mannerisms. Her ability to play drunkenness without losing Sheila's underlying personality makes the sequence especially memorable.

Playing Kate McCallister in the first two Home Alone movies required O'Hara to balance broad family comedy with the increasingly frantic emotions of a mother who has accidentally left her youngest child behind. Considering how ridiculous the premise becomes, her performance is essential to making the situation believable.

In the original film, Kate's gradual realization that Kevin (Macaulay Culkin) is missing culminates in her unforgettable scream of his name. O'Hara makes the moment hilarious through its sheer desperation.

The sequel gives her another opportunity to explore that same panic. Her determination to get back to her son provides the emotional backbone to the movies, offering the ideal counterbalance to the increasingly elaborate slapstick surrounding him.

O'Hara brings genuine warmth to Kate's reunion with Kevin, particularly in the original film's final moments. Her ability to make the character simultaneously exasperated, loving, and completely overwhelmed is a major reason the Home Alone movies are still so enjoyable.

Tim Burton's Beetlejuice gave O'Hara one of her most distinctive film characters ever in Delia Deetz. Delia is an aspiring artist with pretentious sensibilities who moves into the home of a recently deceased couple, Adam and Barbara Maitland (Alec Baldwin and Geena Davis).

Delia is determined to transform the property into a showcase for her avant-garde artistic vision. She is completely convinced of her own sophistication, even when her creative decisions are utterly bewildering to everyone around her.

Her interactions with Winona Ryder's Lydia are particularly enjoyable, as Delia repeatedly attempts to impose her artistic philosophy on a stepdaughter who has absolutely no interest in participating. Importantly, O'Hara gives Delia an exaggerated sense of self-importance without turning her into a conventional villain.

The unforgettable dinner-party sequence demonstrates her physical comedy at its finest. When the guests become possessed and begin singing Harry Belafonte's "Day-O (The Banana Boat Song)," O'Hara delivers a brilliant performance through her facial expressions and precisely synchronized movements. Delia is wonderfully ridiculous, and O'Hara's commitment makes her one of Beetlejuice's standout elements.

Moira Rose is O'Hara's definitive comedic creation, bringing together virtually every strength she developed throughout her career. In Schitt's Creek, she plays a former soap opera star whose wealthy family loses its fortune and is forced to relocate to a small town they purchased as a joke.

Moira's response to her circumstances is consistently hilarious. Her vocabulary, elaborate wardrobe, and seemingly endless collection of wigs make her look as though she has arrived from an entirely different television program. However, O'Hara's performance goes considerably further than making an extravagant character look ridiculous.

Her vocal delivery is extraordinary, particularly the deliberately unusual pronunciations that turn ordinary words into elaborate theatrical performances. Even something as simple as saying "bébé" becomes a memorable comic moment. Her attempt to advertise Herb Ertlinger's fruit wine produces one of the show's funniest sequences.

Moira's relationship with her children, David (Dan Levy) and Alexis (Annie Murphy), also gives O'Hara plenty of opportunities to demonstrate her emotional range. Beneath the vanity and theatrical self-absorption is a mother who genuinely loves her family, even if expressing that affection rarely comes naturally.

More importantly, Moira brings together Catherine O’Hara’s extraordinary vocal comedy, physical expressiveness, and ability to find humanity in even the most ridiculous personalities. It's a fitting showcase for one of comedy's most distinctive performers.

#3488. How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’

Editor’s Note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures opened “Wild Horse Nine” in select theaters on November 6.

While early “Wild Horse Nine” press screenings in Los Angeles and New York got the ball rolling, the first whiff of a strong public reaction was the Venice Film Festival, where edgy auteur Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich, and Sam Rockwell soaked up sustained applause. Then they were whisked to the Colorado Rockies to screen the movie in Telluride.

Instantly, Malkovich jumped up the Best Actor rankings for what would be his third Oscar nomination. His first two were for Supporting Actor, in 1985 for “Places in the Heart,” and 1993 for “In the Line of Fire.” Now the movie is screening at the Toronto International Film Festival ahead of its November 6 release. Related Stories ‘Half Nelson’ at 20: How a $700,000 Indie Addiction Drama Earned Ryan Gosling His First Oscar Nod Cinematographers’ Favorite Festival Is All About AI This Year — but Artists Still Hate the Tech

I caught up with Malkovich in the back of a large black SUV parked in front of the Herzog Theatre before his first of two Telluride Tributes.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Anne Thompson: How did you first get to know Martin McDonagh?

John Malkovich: I was offered a couple things of Martin’s over the years. One, “Seven Psychopaths,” one, [the play] “A Behanding in Spokane,” but I couldn’t do it. I was busy. I love the scripts, but I couldn’t do it, and so then this came. I thought the thing was great. Beautiful piece of writing, just a perfect screenplay, and I couldn’t believe I got sent it. I couldn’t believe he asked me to do it.

Yeah. So I said, “Yeah!” with no hesitation at all. I have two little granddaughters. I don’t love being away for two, three months, whatever. But it’s part of the job, so you got to do it. We met in London because I’d never met Martin. We rehearsed five to six days in London with Sam, who I love. I’d worked with him before on “The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy,” not a long gig, but I knew Sam a bit socially. And I’d worked with Buscemi before twice because he was in our film “Ghost World,” and we worked together in “Con Air.” Sam and I hit it off, workwise, very well, very quickly.

You may not agree, but I think Sam receded slightly and supported you in an amazing way. I find it moving, actually, that he did this for you. Do you feel that’s what he did?

Yes and no. I think he played his part. And the part [of Lee] is slightly recessive in that sense. Chris is the older one. He’s the wild card. He’s killed whatever, 168 people, but apparently none while they were eating. And he’s a legend in the CIA. Sam is an exceptionally generous actor, as generous as you could ever find, you couldn’t ask for a better partner in every way.

You’ve been doing this a long time. Your first Oscar nomination was in 1985. That’s over 40 years ago. Both your nominations have been for Supporting Actor. Are you a character actor?

I’ve had leading roles. But people don’t understand what a role is, the general public or anybody except actors. First of all, you can be a terrific actor in anything, but if the film isn’t good, it’s utterly meaningless. You may as well not have bothered. You may as well not have done it. It’s a waste of time. For a good role to be really good, people have to not just like the way you do that, but like what the character is doing, and understand it if they don’t like it, and they have to like the arc of the character. The best performances I gave would have been on stage first of all, but secondly, those in the cinema wouldn’t necessarily be in good movies, ugh. And that, on a certain level, has precious little to do with performance X, Y, Z. That’s just one small part of a movie.

In this case, you’re given an extraordinary amount of verbiage. So you had to make the rhythm of it, the sense of it, the emotion of it. Sometimes it’s hilariously funny, sometimes sad, and you run that gamut.

Yeah, but that’s great writing. This material, I believe, causes a big wave, and you ride that wave where it’s going, through comedy, through drama, through tragedy, even if that’s the nature of a particular text, and that’s what actors do. The collision between the public and the material is caused by a recognition in their lives.

Our CIA agent Chris is messing around with Chile in 1973 as Pinochet waits in the wings.

November 22, 1963 is a trauma, as is September 11, 2001, and 1973 in Chile. For those of us who were alive at that time, it’s immutable. Doesn’t matter your politics then or now, or if you had any. Doesn’t matter anything. I directed Don DeLillo’s great novel “Libra,” adapted it for the stage with Don, and Don referred to it in the book as the seven seconds that broke the back of the American century in Chile and it was not the only place on earth: Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador.

And various actors have been bad along with us, and possibly not worse, but the birthday party was spoiled. What’s left, and it caused generations of pain, of nihilism, of loss of innocence, of loss of faith in a political system. People everywhere can understand that, and Martin mines that beautifully. It’s beautifully structured in the writing and modulated in the filmmaking. So the wave is there.

Your character is fun to watch because he’s unfettered, he’s unleashed, he doesn’t give a fuck anymore. He’s just going to say what he wants to say, and he’s going to tell the truth.

And people appreciate that because in this culture, it’s very odd. You say this word or that word, and the anti-social media mob goes berserk. I don’t have social media. I don’t want it designated to me in the slightest. I don’t care what they say. They can say whatever they want, and so can people who offend you. They can say whatever they want, and voila, who cares? And this idea that you can’t say that because it’s offensive to this or that, and covers everything and every topic and every subject and every blah blah blah seems incredibly dumb. It’s a dumb world.

Well, that’s one of the great things about being a certain age, right? You don’t care anymore. He doesn’t, and maybe you don’t.

I stay off [social media] because I don’t see the value. I’m doing things. If people like them, beautiful. If they hate them, beautiful. I do a [stage and short film] piece called “The Music Critic,” which is all the worst reviews of all the most beautiful pieces of classical music in the world. They were all trashed. They were all hated. So what? Get used to it. Grow a thick skin, go on with your life, do what you think is good.

#3486. These Surprisingly Powerful Soundcore Earbuds Are Under $35 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3484. HBO Max and Paramount+ Are Officially Headed for the End of an Era

It's been just over a month since the merger between Skydance and Warner Bros. was finalized, yet the full impact of the over $110 billion megadeal is only just beginning to be felt. David Ellison's combined media giant agreed to produce and release a slate of at least 30 films a year, which should be easy to accomplish with both WB and Paramount remaining creatively independent from one another and 2027 already having 36 projects lined up. To fit the companies together, however, Skydance is seeking to cut $6 billion in costs, which has so far resulted in layoffs across all sectors of the company, most recently at Skydance Games. Changes are also coming to the company's streaming strategy.

On Monday, the company shared in its latest quarterly earnings report that it will begin packaging HBO Max and Paramount+ in a "single bundle" that will provide access to both streamers for better value starting in early 2027. That's no real surprise, considering Warner Bros. was already aggressive in bundling its platform with competitors, but this combination is particularly meaningful. It's described as a "first step toward bringing together Paramount+ and HBO Max" into one "fully unified offering." Since the merger, Ellison has been vocal about wanting to marry the two under a single service, but details are scarce on how that will be done exactly. At the very least, Skydance believes the timeline for aligning the two platforms' backends will be quicker than how long it took to integrate Pluto TV with Paramount+.

Combining the two platforms will be a tall task for Skydance, considering the technological lift such an app will require. There's an understandable fear that, like with HBO Max's merger with Discovery+, there will be a wave of content removals to consolidate the two forces. So far, though, no date is set for this union, and no strategy has been publicly shared as to how it'll be accomplished. However, there's confidence the company's new tools and experience with Pluto TV will also lead to a quicker process for creating one app that will bring shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Pitt, and Lanterns under the same roof as the wider Star Trek and Yellowstone universes once the backend systems are in line. The company wrote in its letter to shareholders:

“The integration of Pluto TV with Paramount+ took about 18 months. Drawing on that experience, our combined technology team, and the latest in AI tools, we expect to bring Paramount+ and HBO Max together much faster, aiming to align our backend systems within a year of closing, enabling us to quickly deliver a unified product.”

More details about the Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle and the future of the two platforms will be shared in the coming months. Stay tuned here at Collider for further updates.

#3483. From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

From “Project Hail Mary” to “La Bola Negra” and “You Can See Everything,” this awards season is dominated by director duos.

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, better known as Los Javis, are seen as locks for “La Bola Negra,” the Netflix-backed gay historical epic, while longtime collaborators Phil Lord and Chris Miller are also firmly in the Oscar conversation for their work on “Project Hail Mary.” Then there’s Emmy nominee Nathan Fielder teaming up with documentary-world wunderkind Lance Oppenheim on “You Can See Everything,” a less conventional contender, but one that could muscle itself into the race thanks to its box office success. Related Stories How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’ ‘Half Nelson’ at 20: How a $700,000 Indie Addiction Drama Earned Ryan Gosling His First Oscar Nod

Expand the scope further, and there’s recent indie box office success “Wicker” from husband-and-wife filmmaking duo Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. Plus “Clarissa” from brothers Arie and Chuko Esiri, and “Mouse” from director couple Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson, which picked up a Gotham Best Feature nom.

That’s six different films in this year’s awards conversation, suggesting director duos are becoming more common in filmmaking overall. But in terms of Oscar recognition, only five films across the Academy Awards‘ 98-year history have had their filmmaker duos nominated for Best Director. More than one team nominated for Best Director this season would be a record.

So what makes director duos so rare at the Oscars? Much of it comes down to the Directors Guild of America. Keep in mind, Best Director nominations are determined by the contenders’ peers in the Directors Branch, so even though the DGA is a separate group with its own eligibility rules for the DGA Awards, the guild overlaps enough with the Academy to set the tone. The DGA also has a bylaw that states, “One Director to a Film.” The logic behind the rule, established in 1978, is to prevent anyone, especially producers, from delegating tasks to other members of a director’s team. Director duos can request a waiver, but they must prove they intend to be lifelong collaborators.

The “One Director to a Film” mentality is another major hurdle for “You Can See Everything” directors Fielder and Oppenheim in particular, as both filmmakers had established solo careers before teaming up. Meanwhile, the rest of the class of 2026 director duos have been collaborators from the start of their careers, with Los Javis and Lord and Miller, the two most viable Best Director candidates, even having shorthand nicknames within the industry. “You Can See Everything” has already been deemed ineligible for a Best Director nomination at the DGA Awards, because the category does not include documentaries.

Despite the hurdles they must overcome, director duos often go on to win Oscars if they secure a nomination. That was the case for “West Side Story” directors Robert Wise and Jerome Robbins in 1962, for “No Country for Old Men” directors Joel and Ethan Coen in 2008, and most recently for “Everything Everywhere All at Once” directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (aka Daniels) in 2023.

Of the two director duos that fell short, one was the Coen Brothers again for “True Grit” in 2011, only three years after they won the Best Director Oscar. That makes “Heaven Can Wait” helmers Warren Beatty and Buck Henry the only director duo that didn’t win the Oscar the first time they were nominated as a pair. Henry and Beatty would never direct together again, and Beatty would win the Oscar for directing “Reds” three years after “Heaven Can Wait” came out in 1978.

So while there’s a tremendous barrier for entry, if any of the director duos in the awards mix this year are able to secure a Best Director nomination, history indicates they should probably have an acceptance speech ready.

#3482. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3480. Harlan Coben Will Officially Replace The Lincoln Lawyer In 2027

Netflix’s adaptation of The Lincoln Lawyer has thrilled audiences for almost five years, but now it’s drawing to a close. The next season of maverick lawyer Mickey Haller’s story will be his last new case on the streaming platform. The literary half-brother of fellow Prime Video’s Harry Bosch is being retired from streaming, it seems.

Season 5 of The Lincoln Lawyer will be released in March, after which Mickey’s detective sister Emi Finch is getting her own Netflix spinoff series, but he’ll be nothing more than a bit-part player in her story. Meanwhile, the streaming giant’s next multi-season adaptation of a hugely popular literary character – who also happens to have trained as a lawyer – is just getting started.

However, his 14th Netflix series will be a very different story. David E. Kelley and Kyle Long’s as-yet untitled Myron Bolitar project brings the character who launched Coben’s literary career to the screen for the very first time. What’s more, he’s going to front the first multiseason serial drama Coben has ever agreed to.

Netflix’s Myron Bolitar series was only confirmed back in May 2026, yet it’s already wrapped filming, and is slated for release at some point in 2027. We can expect it to follow hot on the heels of The Lincoln Lawyer’s final season, giving those in need of a good procedural mystery something similarly gripping to get hooked on.

The protagonist of 12 novels by Harlan Coben, including his 1995 breakout success Deal Breaker, Myron Bolitar is a would-be basketballer whose childhood dream of turning professional is suddenly ended by a freak injury. He turns his attention instead to becoming a sports agent, after qualifying as a lawyer from Harvard.

Harlan Coban is one of contemporary crime fiction's most prolific authors; these are the thrillers and mysteries he's been reading the last few years.

Bolitar isn’t just a taller, literary version of Jerry Maguire, though. His quick wits, keen eye for detail, rough-and-ready approach to work, and insistence on a stringent moral code, invariably take him down a rabbit hole of crime investigation, too. In fact, it’s a wonder he didn’t set out to be a private eye in the first place.

The upcoming TV adaptation of Coben’s Myron Bolitar novels will star The Continental’s Colin Woodell as its central character, alongside familiar faces such as Chloe Fineman (Saturday Night Live) and Jabari Banks (Bel-Air). Funnily enough, it also features two actors who’ve made appearances in The Lincoln Lawyer.

Besides Netflix’s Myron Bolitar adaptation borrowing Jamie McShane and Diane Guerrero from The Lincoln Lawyer, where they play Detective Lee Lankford and a season 5 character called Natalia, respectively, it looks set to steal the thunder from Mickey Haller’s last case in 2027. As Harlan Coben’s first show with multiple seasons, it’s bound to wrack up serious viewing numbers on streaming for several years to come.

Coben has had two different global number 1 hits on Netflix in 2026 alone, in the miniseries adaptations Run Away and I Find You. His most celebrated literary creation’s screen debut will be on a whole other level, though. It’s no accident that producers appear to have fast-tracked the rollout of this series to coincide with the end of The Lincoln Lawyer’s run.

Myron Bolitar’s arrival on Netflix appears to be specifically designed to replace the massive success of its flagship legal thriller, with David E. Kelley on board, no less. The similarities between Bolitar and Mickey Haller are uncanny. Both are uncompromising mavericks whose legal qualifications often conflict with their unorthodox approaches to ensuring justice is served, founded on morals they fiercely defend.

Myron and Mickey are both at their happiest enjoying their sports as well, whether it’s basketball or surfing. The Lincoln Lawyer might be ending next year, but fans can rest assured there’s already someone out there preparing to fill the void Mickey Haller will leave behind. It’s time for Michael Connelly to step aside. Harlan Coben’s best-loved protagonist is taking center stage.

#3479. DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down as Co-CEOs, Marvel Vet Jeremy Latcham Named Chief Creative Officer

James Gunn and Peter Safran are out as heads of DC Studios.

The move comes after Skydance closed its $110 billion deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery in October. Jeremy Latcham, who helped shape the Marvel Cinematic Universe, has been appointed president and chief creative officer, DC Studios, beginning December 1, 2026.

Gunn and Safran joined the company four years ago with the goal of making DC a true challenger to the MCU, but they’ve had mixed success. “Superman,” which Gunn directed, was a hit at the box office, but “Supergirl” bombed and “Clayface,” an R-rated body horror film, has performed modestly. The pair also launched new series based on the comic book company’s characters, including “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns.” Gunn has one more film on the horizon, the “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow,” which opens next year. Related Stories James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next ‘Clayface’ Tops the Box Office with $24 Million. What Does It Signal About DC Studios’ Latest Reboot?

“James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of,” David Ellison, Chairman and CEO, and Ynon Kreiz, Co-CEO, of Skydance said in a statement. “We’re grateful for their passion, contributions, and commitment to this legendary brand. Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans.”

In a separate statement, Gunn and Safran said, “Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore ‘Superman’ to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with ‘Peacemaker,’ ‘Creature Commandos,’ ‘Lanterns,’ and ‘Clayface.’ We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews, and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter.”

Latcham will lead DC’s film, television, and animation slate. He will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, Co-Chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

“Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” said Goldberg and Greenstein. “Under his leadership, every film and television show will be ushered from start to finish through the prism of the legions of fans who love and champion it. Jeremy’s track record exemplifies the excellence he will bring to building out DC and the many beloved characters within it.”

At Marvel, Latcham produced several of the company’s biggest hits, including “The Avengers,” “Spider-Man: Homecoming,” “Iron Man 2,” and “Guardians of the Galaxy,” which Gunn directed. As an independent producer, his credits include “Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves” and “The Breadwinner.”

Latcham faces a steep challenge. DC has suffered from a lack of consistency in its creative direction. The studio was initially overseen by comic book veterans Geoff Johns and Jon Berg, who were later replaced by veteran producer Walter Hamada, before he too was ousted. Over that time, DC had hits such as “Aquaman” and “Wonder Woman,” but they were outweighed by costly failures like “Justice League” and “The Flash.”

When Discovery bought Warner Bros. in 2022, David Zaslav personally courted Gunn and Safran to turn the ship around. But the timing was tricky. Comic book movies remain popular, at least the ones featuring marquee heroes like Spider-Man or Batman, but audiences have grown more discerning. They are less likely to show up for second- or third-tier characters (see: Supergirl). So it will fall to Latcham to figure out a new strategy to meet the moment, one that either builds on Gunn and Safran’s foundation or takes the studio in yet another direction.

#3478. The JBL Vibe Beam Earbuds Are on Sale for $30 Right Now

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. Ten minutes of charging will get you a couple of hours of playback, and they have an IP54 rating, making them dust- and splash-resistant. The built-in mics work well in reasonably quiet rooms, but may struggle to separate your voice from loud background noise. With 8 mm dynamic drivers, they deliver punchy bass that translates well to adrenaline-pumping workout music, and adequate vocal clarity for music and podcasts. Though the default tuning is relatively balanced, you can tweak it on the app’s equalizer to adjust it to your liking. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

#3477. Clint Eastwood’s True-Crime Thriller Is Officially Netflix’s Next ‘Mindhunter’

There's something about these true-crime stories that gets us particularly riled up and curious, isn't there? After all, truth is stranger than fiction and so on, and so forth. And we love them, don't we? Netflix has made an entire industry out of exploring complicated investigations, miscarriages of justice, and the darker corners of American criminal history, but few of its productions have left quite the same impression as Mindhunter. And while fans are still mourning the loss of David Fincher's extraordinary psychological thriller, one of Clint Eastwood's most overlooked movies has just arrived to help fill the void.

Eastwood's 2019 true-crime drama Richard Jewell has officially landed on Netflix in the United States, joining the platform on November 1. The movie is based on one of the most stunning and dramatic crime sagas in recent American history, exploring how an ordinary American hero ended up at the center of one of the country's biggest ever criminal investigations.

The world is first introduced to Richard Jewell (Paul Walter Hauser) as the security guard who reports finding the device during the 1996 Atlanta bombing – his report making him a hero whose swift actions saved countless lives. But within days, the law enforcement wannabe becomes the FBI’s number one suspect, vilified by press and public alike, his life ripped apart. Reaching out to independent, anti-establishment attorney Watson Bryant (Sam Rockwell), Jewell staunchly professes his innocence. But Bryant finds he is out of his depth as he fights the combined powers of the FBI, GBI and APD to clear his client’s name, while keeping Richard from trusting the very people trying to destroy him.

The cast stars Hauser (Black Bird) and Rockwell (Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri), alongside Kathy Bates (Misery) as Bobi Jewell, Jon Hamm (Mad Men) as Tom Shaw, Olivia Wilde (House) as Kathy Scruggs, Nina Arianda (Goliath) as Nadya, Ian Gomez (Cougar Town) as Agent Dan Bennet, and Dylan Kussman (Dead Poets Society) as Bruce Hughes.

The film earned approximately $22.3 million domestically and holds a 77% critics' score and 96% verified audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Bates also received an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress.

#3476. CleanMyMac now helps you clean up Gmail and manage Chrome tabs

MacPaw today announced an expansion of CleanMyMac’s capabilities beyond the app’s traditional Mac maintenance and optimization tools. Here are the details.

CleanMyMac got two new features today, Email Cleanup and Browser Care, which are “designed to help users tackle digital clutter throughout their workday,” MacPaw explains.

Interestingly, both features focus on Google services, with Email Cleanup targeting Gmail and Browser Care designed specifically for Chrome.

Email Cleanup also helps users identify emails taking up storage space shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos, allowing them to reclaim it once those messages are permanently deleted.

As for Browser Care, it “helps users reclaim Mac memory and stay focused by identifying Google Chrome tabs that consume valuable resources or create unnecessary clutter,” according to the company’s press release.

It works via a Chrome browser extension that connects directly to CleanMyMac, and lets users access “near real-time,” as MacPaw put it, “memory usage, pause resource-intensive tabs, find duplicates across browser windows and identify pages that have been left open for hours or days.”

In practice, MacPaw says, Browser Care makes it easier to identify which background tabs are affecting the Mac’s performance, helping users address slowdowns and reduce distractions.

MacPaw also emphasizes that Email Cleanup requires confirmation before making changes, while Browser Care only closes or suspends tabs when users choose to do so. The company adds that page content, titles, and browsing history remain stored locally on the Mac.

Both features are rolling out today to users with an active CleanMyMac subscription. To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.

#3475. Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?

Don’t be surprised if you emerge from Alex Thompson and Kelly O’Sullivan’s piercingly moving coming-of-age grief dramedy “Mouse” in a puddle of tears. Graceful in technique, compassionate in its writing, this movie, one of the year’s best, is a crying machine. But that’s not to say this story of a high school girl’s (Katherine Mallen Kupferer, astonishing) formative first encounter with major loss is any bit manipulative.

As heartbreak ripples through a small town, “Mouse” has the texture and deep feeling of Kenneth Lonergan’s post-9/11 New York City drama “Margaret,” starring Anna Paquin as a precocious teenager in freefall after witnessing a pedestrian’s brutal death. Unlike “Margaret,” “Mouse” didn’t take over half a decade to reach screens after production wrapped, but the road was still paved with rejection (baffling in retrospect) for Chicago directing duo Thompson and O’Sullivan. Related Stories From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’

With “Mouse,” the filmmakers found themselves at the Berlin Film Festival for the first time back in February — even as an American indie set in Arkansas about the challenges of coming of age feels like catnip for a festival like Sundance, where such topics are historically de rigueur. And Thompson and O’Sullivan had been to Sundance before, with their critically championed 2024 comedy-drama “Ghostlight,” about an emotionally ramshackle, rookie community theater production of “Romeo and Juliet.” While placement at the legacy indie festival, headed to Boulder in January, doesn’t always mean you’re grandfathered into the acceptance pipeline for your next movie, it was still a surprise to the directors (who are also life partners with two children) when Sundance turned down “Mouse” not once, but twice.

“To be totally fair, we submitted before we probably should have, with a long cut,” O’Sullivan told IndieWire over Zoom. “Apparently, it didn’t matter,” Thompson added.

“We submitted it again the next year, when it was tighter,” added O’Sullivan, though the filmmakers were dismissed again. “The feedback that we got — and again, this is a game of telephone, so we don’t know — is that it had real champions, but that it also had people who didn’t get it. Yes, it was crushing. It was confusing. More than anything, I was like, ‘Wait, but people did such great work on this movie. The work is incredible.’ And not ours even, but Sophie [Okonedo] and Katherine [Mallen Kupferer], and the crew, I was like, ‘I feel like they deserve a really big stage.’”

Luckily, the Berlin Film Festival stepped in to program “Mouse” in the Panorama section, marking Thompson and O’Sullivan’s first bow at a European fest, where it grabbed strong reviews. And, as the filmmakers point out, that festival turned out to be the proper home. (Berlin, after all, just had its strongest lineup in years, under artistic director Tricia Tuttle’s second festival.)

“It really was hard for a moment, and then we heard back from Berlin, and it kind of felt like a career opportunity that went way beyond Sundance,” Thompson said. “Tapping into the narrative outside of the American indie felt like something we’d always aspired to. And those are the films that I identify with the most, the sort of work that comes out of those great European festivals. The most jealous and childish I am is every year when the Venice reviews start coming out, and it’s like, ‘Ah, well, those all sound great.’ And Cannes and Berlin, and our favorite festivals, we have a relationship with Thessaloniki and American Film Festival in Wrocław, and to have that stage at Berlin, it’s like this sort of historic stage. It’s absolutely mind-blowing. I’ve never been in a theater that big with a movie.”

A Gotham nominee for Best Feature, “Mouse” is now quietly in theaters from Independent Film Company. (A sparsely attended Academy screening also took place in Los Angeles over the weekend.) Film chatterers may deem this a “small” movie in a year of “You Can See Everything” and “La Bola Negra,” it is huge in every way.

The film follows Minnie Dunn (Kupferer), who, just as she’s about to enter her senior year, is dealt a life-altering loss. It’s 2002, Michelle Branch is on the radio, and September 11 is not even a year out of view. Faced with a hole in her life in the shape of her lifelong best friend after a tragic accident, Minnie forms a tight bond with the girl’s British stay-at-home mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo, luminescent here), mourning on her own. Meanwhile, Minnie’s classmates all but literally compete to see who can grieve the loudest in the form of a talent show. “Mouse” is about the centrifugal force of grief and how life goes on around you, but you’re still stuck in the same place.

Big on emotional generosity and ace turns from the filmmakers’ stable of theater-based Chicago actors — including Kupferer and her real-life mother Tara Mallen, who plays Minnie’s struggling, lower-middle-class mom onscreen — “Mouse” deserves as much attention as any of the year’s best films. The grand ambition of “Mouse” and its emotional dividends and wonderful performances suggest it could’ve cleaned up at Telluride or even Toronto, where, in the latter case, a number of indie films flopped, and even the most acclaimed are still searching for distribution.

“Rejected, rejected,” O’Sullivan laughed, later adding, “We understand how complicated programming a festival is, and we don’t feel entitled to be programmed anywhere. We’re grateful to every festival that’s given us a slot.”

She wrote the script for “Mouse” in 2019, around the time their debut feature as collaborators, “Saint Frances,” opened at SXSW. That microbudget indie, directed by Thompson and starring O’Sullivan as a drifting 34-year-old nanny in Chicago, won the Austin festival’s audience award and later earned a John Cassavetes Spirit Award nomination. “Mouse” was actually meant to be their next feature, with one financier, a cushier budget, and a slightly different cast — until the strikes changed their plans, leading to “Ghostlight” as their Sundance debut on a smaller scale.

Based on O’Sullivan’s own experience with loss as a teen, “Mouse” picked back up in fall 2024, shooting on location in her home state of Arkansas. “We were amazingly able to retain the vision” of “Mouse” from before the strikes, she said. “Nothing got cut for budget.”

Thompson, who produced the film, said, “Knowing the budget so intimately, I guess that’s my superpower on the producing side that most directors don’t have is I just get really intimate with the budget. And it seems really boring, but it’s kind of like a script where if you don’t have the means, if it’s not there in the budget, it’s not going to happen… A lot of directors I talked to have been like, ‘Oh, well, my producer said we couldn’t do a rain tower, or my producers said we couldn’t do this shot because we can’t afford it.’ And it’s like, well, you can pretty much afford anything. You just have to give somewhere else. We tend to make really ambitious one-liners like schedules. We had 30 days on this, but that ended up being a two-hour and 15-minute movie, and we cut 20 minutes.”

When asked about the “Mouse” budget, he said, “I think we can say. We’re already underdogs. We might as well say. It was $3 million.”

And it’s $3 million, well-budgeted and in true indie spirit — like a scene where Minnie and her friends watch “Titanic” in a parent’s basement during one of those classic sleepovers where private confidences spill out, insulated from the adult world upstairs and outside.

“We didn’t even try to get the rights to ‘Titanic,’ but we’re mixing at Skywalker,” Thompson said. “They have the entire effects library for ‘Titanic’ … so we rebuilt the dance scene in ‘Titanic’ and used public-domain Irish music, and then Kelly and [producer] Pierce Cravens do the voices of Leo and Kate off in a room being like, ‘I feel so young,’ or something, whatever that is. If you watch the movie, you think they’re watching ‘Titanic’ in the basement, but it’s a totally constructed thing because we’re like, ‘We can’t get the rights to this.'”

On top of “Mouse” already dwelling on a very specific point of loss from O’Sullivan’s own childhood, the filmmaker’s mother also died in Arkansas toward the end of production. That meant she was actively grieving while also leading a set, alongside her partner.

“It was so bizarre,” O’Sullivan said. “She died when we had a week and a half left to shoot… It was incredibly complicated. I just couldn’t believe the timing of it for so many different reasons. I mean, one of which is just that it took forever to make this movie, but the movie allowed me to be there literally when she died. I didn’t have to get on a plane. But then when I was back on set, I just kept hearing these lines that I had written, and they took on a whole new meaning… lines that I had sort of written in a very theoretical way all of a sudden were hitting me in a, ‘God, I can’t believe how true this was, and I didn’t even know.'”

The autobiography that drove “Mouse” extended behind the scenes in even more literal ways. Christen Pitts, the choreographer behind the movie’s climactic ballet elegy sequence set to a cover of Cyndi Lauper’s “Time After Time,” was O’Sullivan’s high school dance teacher. “It feels like so many different chapters of my life are just compressing into the same space, and it feels like a culmination of my entire adult life and teenage years and echoes of the past existing,” O’Sullivan said.

Thompson and O’Sullivan have maintained their filmmaking footprint in and around Chicago — even as “Mouse” brought them to Arkansas — and they don’t feel especially tempted to make the leap to Hollywood, though there have been offers.

“I just write from a place of experience most of the time, and I don’t know, I’ve seen so many movies set in L.A. and New York, and I actually don’t identify with those towns,” O’Sullivan said. “I feel like enough people are doing that, and I like writing from a place of specificity … I’ve spent maybe a year in both places cumulatively. It doesn’t feel like a character that I personally need to explore. But having said that, if I spent more time there, it felt like a story was necessarily set there. I’d be open to it. I just don’t feel compelled to.”

“We really want to have a body of work,” Thompson said. “The people I admire the most are Steven Soderbergh and Sidney Lumet, directors who have dozens of films by the time they stop, and Soderbergh has not stopped, obviously.” He doesn’t know that a move to Los Angeles is possible given their artistic goals. “We’ve gone out on meetings, we’ve done pitches, we’ve considered projects from studios, and the timeline always felt kind of like it just hasn’t really worked out. ‘Mouse’ was so close to being that thing, and then the writers’ strike, and the SAG strike, we lost a cast member, and it just all fell away. So we just thought, ‘What if we just do what we did on ‘Ghostlight,’ but on steroids? If I can raise half a million dollars, I wonder if we can raise three.”

With the filmmakers now set up at Gersh talent agency, he added, “If we want to make a movie every 15 months, we probably can’t do that in the studio system. But I think we both like the idea of playing in a bigger sandbox and taking the intimacy, taking all the things we’ve learned, and working in a bigger sandbox. I don’t think that’s unattractive, but it’s just, for the way we work, this has made the most sense so far.”

Next up, Thompson directed a high-concept body-swap comedy starring the “Ghostlight” father-daughter (and real-life father-daughter) team of “Mouse” star Katherine Mallen Kupferer with Keith Kupferer. Plus, they’ve co-directed “The Steel Harp,” starring Lois Smith and O’Sullivan in a return to acting. Both are expected in 2027.

“We shoot on the same lenses as ‘Saint Frances,’ same aspect ratio as ‘Mouse,’ in a world that winks at a bigger sandbox,” Thompson said of the body swap movie. “It’s a total gamble. I’ve got no idea if it’s going to work… It seems to be quite funny according to my three-year-old.”

“Mouse” is now playing in New York and Los Angeles, with a wider expansion to follow in November.

#3474. Report: Apple captured half of global smartphone revenue in Q3

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, Apple just recorded its highest-ever global smartphone revenue for a third calendar quarter. Here are the details.

In a report released earlier this week, Counterpoint Research mapped out the global smartphone market’s performance during the third quarter, which saw Apple capture its highest-ever share of industry revenue for the period.

Samsung, which came in second, accounted for 19% of global smartphone revenue, followed by Xiaomi at 6%, OPPO at 5%, and vivo at 4%.

In another record, Counterpoint says Apple saw the iPhone average selling price (ASP) hit an all-time-high of $1,031, up 19% year-over-year.

Counterpoint’s Research Director Tarun Pathak explained that the iPhone 18 Pro series contributed to Apple’s ASP growth, despite launching toward the end of the third calendar quarter:

“Apple remained the most resilient major brand in Q3 2026, with shipments nearly flat YoY. Apple has the pricing power to absorb rising memory costs and pass them on to consumers with minimal impact on demand. At the same time, ASP growth was supported by higher launch prices for the iPhone 18 Pro series, the absence of the base iPhone 18 from the launch and price increases across older models in September. Together, these factors helped Apple deliver strong revenue growth in an otherwise challenging market.”

Finally, the report noted that while Samsung still led the market in shipment share, its lead over Apple narrowed slightly, with the companies accounting for 22% and 21% of global smartphone shipments, respectively.

#3473. Gilmore Girls: Every Main Character's Ending, Ranked

There's nothing that Gilmore Girls fans like better than a debate about the fates of the characters on the show. There's no shortage of discourse about the way every main character's arc ends. Some characters got satisfying, beautiful conclusions that made long-time viewers emotional. However, others left us disappointed, as even if their development made sense, it was still hard to watch.

Every episode of A Year in the Life delves into the lives of not only the Gilmores but also their loved ones and the residents of Stars Hollow. It's a nostalgic return to the town and the beloved characters, as well as an opportunity for the series to right some wrongs that happened in the original series. There are some harsh realities of being a Gilmore Girls fan, as the characters don't always make the decisions we want them to, but many character arcs come full circle in the series.

Lane is one of the best and most underrated characters in all of Gilmore Girls, and there's a general consensus that she deserved a lot better than her ending in Gilmore Girls. After Zack nearly destroys the band's chances of making it big, Lane ends up marrying him and then almost immediately getting pregnant. After working so hard to establish an independent life and break out of her mother's constraints, Lane ends up with a life she didn't initially intend for.

Of course, she loves her children and family, and she does seem content in A Year in the Life, but Lane deserved to see the world as a musician and leave Stars Hollow like she always dreamed of. Lane had just as much promise as Rory and was ready to work even harder than her friend to achieve her dreams. Lane should've had a different ending and gotten credit for being such a standout character in the series.

It's simultaneously true that Rory's arc on Gilmore Girls and A Year in the Life was disappointing and also deeply accurate. From the beginning of the series, it's hinted that Rory is doomed to repeat the same cycle of mistakes characteristic of the Gilmore family by not living up to the high expectations of others and the great promise she showed when she was young.

To be a high achiever and then struggle to find her place in the world when she isn't constantly handled and sheltered by Lorelai, Emily, and Richard is exactly what was always going to happen to Rory. It's hard to watch her fail and make mistakes as she realizes her life didn't turn out the way she thought it would. However, it's fitting and narratively sound, even if it doesn't make it easy to side with Rory.

Gilmore Girls had a distinctly early-2000s feel, but these actors could make a modern-day remake of the beloved drama feel just as cozy.

As Rory's final boyfriend in Gilmore Girls, and on-and-off flame in A Year in the Life, Logan is one of the most consistent and best-suited romances of Rory's life. It's unfortunate that season 7 undid some of his character development by having him give Rory an ultimatum to marry him and break things off when she wasn't ready. This went against much of the work that audiences saw him do throughout the show.

In A Year in the Life, Logan and Rory are still seeing each other despite Logan's relationship with another woman and Rory's aimless lifestyle. However, it seems that he's found some balance between what's expected of him and what he wants to do with his life. His final adventure with Rory is a touching sendoff for their relationship, and shows that Logan will always have a rebellious streak, even if he's learned how to grow up.

It comes as no surprise that Paris is at the top of her game when we catch up with her in A Year in the Life. It's disappointing that she and Doyle got divorced, but Paris is doing everything she ever set out to do and hasn't lost an ounce of her high-achieving spirit. This is a sharp foil to Rory's floundering, and is a reminder that though Rory often bested Paris when they were young, that dynamic wasn't permanent.

Paris' insults on Gilmore Girls are some of the funniest moments in the show, and the whip-smart character doesn't disappoint audiences in A Year in the Life. She's hilarious and great to spend time with in the revival, even if her anxiety at seeing Tristan again at Chilton was a little unbelievable, since Paris has come so far since high school. Paris as an adult is still intense, but she's a more compassionate and evolved person.

In her breakout role of Sookie in Gilmore Girls, Melissa McCarthy is as charming and hilarious as ever. It was a treat to see McCarthy make a cameo in A Year in the Life​​​​​​, and hear about the amazing work Sookie is doing as a chef in the series. Of course, we wish we got to spend more time with Sookie in the revival, but her appearance provided the nostalgic moment fans needed.

Though it seems like her career and family were in a good place in A Year in the Life, it's hard not to remember the difficulties Sookie faced in Gilmore Girls season 7. Jackson lying about his vasectomy and Sookie's accidental pregnancy is one of the worst parts of the final season. Though the couple works through it, this betrayal taints what was one of the best relationships on the show. The main series sees her pregnant and happy to send Rory off into the world, but we can't forget the trials of season 7.

Michel is one of Gilmore Girls' best scene stealers throughout the series, always providing a quip or sarcastic comment that makes it impossible not to appreciate his character. However, as a more supporting character, his personal life and development outside the Dragonfly Inn and his relationship with Lorelai aren't explored very deeply in the main show.

Fortunately, A Year in the Life not only confirmed that Michel was part of the LGBTQ+ community, but the series also gave him a husband who seemed to be the other half Michel was looking for. It's incredibly satisfying to see this happen for Michel, and it gives him a fitting ending for a character whose romantic life was always implied but never confirmed.

Jess has a few "endings" on Gilmore Girls, as the misunderstood, angry young man whom the Gilmores meet in season 2 changes a lot by the time he returns as an adult. Rory and Jess's romance in Gilmore Girls has been the subject of hot debate for years. When Jess was young, there's no question he didn't treat Rory well, even if he was a romantic bad boy viewers could idealize.

However, it's when Jess comes back in season 6 that viewers can appreciate how vital it was that he grew up and found his purpose. Moving to a new city and following his dreams of writing and working in publishing is the kind of growth that Jess fans were hoping for. However, he continues carrying a torch for Rory throughout season 6 and A Year in the Life, which is compelling for the plot, but it's a part of his character that keeps him stuck in the past.

Watching Luke grapple with his loss of Lorelai and the poor way he handled integrating April into his life in seasons 6 and 7 is a moment of character development for Stars Hollow's diner owner. However, he comes back around to their relationship and learns how to be the partner Lorelai needs, and vice versa.

In A Year in the Life, Luke couldn't be more committed to their life together and is able to weather Lorelai's struggle with finding her life's purpose better than he ever did in the past. He's serious and all in to their relationship and isn't afraid of making this known, telling her how he feels and how important she is in ways he failed to in the original series. For Luke's character, this is a big step, and his marriage to Lorelai is a beautiful full-circle moment for him.

One of the saddest parts of A Year in the Life is the passing of Richard, and this loss and its aftereffects are the primary character for Emily Gilmore. In the main series, the viewer witnesses Emily, the third Gilmore girl, grow as an individual and begin to define herself and her value outside of the traditional rules she was raised with and attempted to pass down to Lorelai and Rory.

Though Emily is far from perfect, even in the later seasons of Gilmore Girls, she becomes more understanding of her daughter and her choices and learns how to have a relationship with her through the repetition of her mistakes with Rory in season 6, when she drops out of Yale. Throughout A Year in the Life, Emily agrees to do therapy sessions with Lorelai, and while they don't always go well, she gains more respect for her daughter and is able to grieve Richard while finding new ways to enjoy her life without him.

After the season 7 finale, audiences could rest assured that Luke and Lorelai ended up the way they were supposed to, so when Lorelai returns for A Year in the Life, her arc had to be deeper than an extension of her will-they-won't-they dynamic with Luke. Of course, Lorelai was always much more than her romantic relationships, and this is clear in her ending. While it hits home when she and Luke finally, officially get married, it's her journey getting there that's the most compelling.

Lorelai achieves actualization and a sense of contentment in her ending, allowing her to fully commit to her life with Luke and let go of some of the anger she was still carrying toward her parents. Though Lorelai will likely continue indulging in some moments of regression in the future, Gilmore Girls gave one of its protagonists a fitting conclusion, allowing her to move forward and support Rory as she figures out her path.

In the fictional town of Star's Hollow, single mother Lorelai Gilmore raises her high-achieving teenage daughter Rory. Mother and daughter rely on each other throughout their own life changes, romantic entanglements, and friendships.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3472. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.
