#3471. Apple expected to bid for F1 streaming rights in more countries, says Formula 1 CEO

On the latest earnings call for F1’s parent company Liberty Media, the CEO of Formula 1 Stefano Domenicali said that both parties are happy with the US deal, and he expects that Apple will bid for rights in more countries as the opportunities become available.

F1 has previously expressed that they are not currently looking for one media partner to take global broadcast rights for the sport; they want a portfolio of deals, picking the best partners for each geographic market.

We have already seen this play out in the United Kingdom, with broadcaster Sky renewing its deal for F1 rights through 2034, seemingly locking Apple out of that region. So, despite the apparent demand, Apple will not be able to just walk in and take over the future of the sport’s worldwide distribution.

However, it seems the league is open to striking more deals with Apple in certain markets.

On the earnings call, in response to a question from an investor about Apple’s interest, Domenicali said “this is part of our discussion, if there are opportunities that can be in other markets, they will do it … they’re going to do it as soon as these opportunities will be open for them”.

Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang said they continue to think about what new innovation they can bring to the product side, and noted that “Apple as a potential bidder in other markets is helpful” for their business.

As a reminder, all Formula 1 races are available to watch live and on-demand with an Apple TV subscription, in the United States. The company recently launched a Dolby Atmos audio track for its F1 streams, as well as expanded support for Multiview on more platforms, including iPhone Duo.

#3470. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3469. Our Plea to the New DC Studios Head: No More Shared Universe!

Four years ago, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran relaunched the comics brand with grand ambitions to build a Marvel Cinematic Universe of their own with a crop of characters they believed to be superior to what Marvel and Disney had. They controlled Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, and a whole bunch more they could mold as they saw fit, and they promised they would fix the flawed Marvel Studios system of greenlighting projects before a strong screenplay was in place. They announced a massive slate of 10 films and series right out of the gate and had other expectations that stars they cast today would appear in future DC films for the long haul. Above all, they were going to be careful with the brand. Related Stories DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down as Co-CEOs, Marvel Vet Jeremy Latcham Named Chief Creative Officer James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

“No one was minding the mint,” Gunn said back in January 2023 in a telling quote. “They were just giving away IP like they were party favors to any creators who smiled at them. What we are going to do is promise that everything from our first project going forward is going to be unified.”

The real world quickly caught up to Gunn and Safran. In a move beyond their control, ownership of DC Studios changed hands yet again from Warner Bros. Discovery to Skydance, and now just four years, three films, and a couple of TV shows into their tenure, they’re out. Taking the reins is Jeremy Latcham, not a household name the way Kevin Feige or some of his lieutenants have been, but an architect of the early stages of the MCU and a key, former executive at Marvel (he left for an independent label of his own in 2017). He has comic book chops, having produced “The Avengers,” the first MCU “Spider-Man,” and more.

Because the ball didn’t really get rolling at DC Studios in the short time Gunn and Safran were on board, and because Latcham still has a lingering slate that includes a second “Superman” movie that’s already in the can and a second “The Batman” movie in the works that isn’t even connected to the DCU anyway, as he begins to map out his own ambitions for the next era of DC movies and series, we have a simple plea: no more shared universes. Please. We beg you. Enough already.

Do not try and build the next MCU or even the next DC(E)U or whatever you want to call it. Just make some really good superhero movies with the characters and brands people love.

Books have been and will be written about the producing success story Kevin Feige managed with the MCU, and David Ellison, fanboy that he is, would surely love to have his own version of “The Avengers.” Who wouldn’t? We’ve seen other studios try and recreate the MCU formula with their own IP, like the Godzilla vs. Kong-iverse from WB and Legendary or the incredibly misguided plan for a Universal monster-verse that fizzled out with Tom Cruise’s “The Mummy.“

Truth be told, Marvel is trying to reconstruct its own formula ever since “Avengers: Endgame,” and it has been a mixed bag. Sure, there were a few billion-dollar hits in there like “Deadpool & Wolverine” and this year’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” and “Avengers: Doomsday” too figures to be huge, but other new characters and would-be franchises like “Eternals” or “Shang-Chi” have gone through fits and stops. Movies like a “Blade” reboot have never been able to get off the ground as Marvel tries to fit a square peg into a round hole. Marvel has been forced to recast and scramble its carefully laid plans amid the controversy around Jonathan Majors. And the sheer glut of TV shows over the last few years has created immense homework for people that has led the actual flagship movies to drop off precipitously at the box office.

Is that what DC Studios really wants? More of that drama and headache? It feels like we’re well beyond the era where audiences are willing to commit for every new episode of a yearslong cinematic saga. Surely whatever vision Gunn and Safran had was grand, especially if you’re a real fan of those characters and want to see them all come together as the Justice League yet again, but it doesn’t feel like today’s young audiences want to sign up for that.

Gunn and Safran actually immediately ran into this problem as they tried to bridge the gap between the old DCEU and the new DCU they were building. People knew “The Flash” and “Aquaman 2” weren’t going to be part of the future, even as Gunn and Safran paid lip service to the idea and played coy about having some of these actors reprising their roles in the new universe. (Remember when Henry Cavill thought for a minute he was playing Superman again?) The films underwhelmed at the box office as a result, and it created confusion among casual fans as the execs were forced to dance around the fanboys and the Snyder Army.

Audiences, though, have demonstrated that superhero movies still matter when they feature characters they care about. “Spider-Man” stayed away for about five years, and “Brand New Day” is now one of the highest-grossing movies of all time. We hadn’t had a proper, standalone “Superman” movie in years, and it proved to be a great launching pad for Gunn’s slate, earning $618.7 million worldwide. There’s still huge excitement for “The Batman: Part II” from Matt Reeves, and there’s never been any pretense that it’s connected to some more important lore or that Pattinson’s Bruce Wayne might show up in a theoretical “Wonder Woman” sequel a decade down the road. People just really like Batman.

So what do you do now if you’re Latcham and have to answer to Ellison and former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz? It would make sense to just demonstrate how you’re going to make the most of the IP that you have. Signaling to audiences (and shareholders) that your next Wonder Woman movie won’t come out until 2037 because you’re mapping out the shared universe for how to carefully introduce all these characters doesn’t sound like the best approach. Just hire smart writers, entrust visionary directors, and make some good movies. It worked with “The Batman.”

This, of course, does not mean don’t make your big “Justice League” team up movie or don’t build a new franchise out of “Teen Titans.” It just means that times and appetites have changed from the pre-Covid and even pre-streaming boom MCU era when “Guardians of the Galaxy” could be a hit (in part) because of how it teased the arrival of Thanos and the Infinity Stones. Audiences have become more discerning about what they define as an event film, and DC Studios can beat Marvel at its own game so long as DC stops trying to become Marvel.

#3468. 3 Best Movies on Prime Video This Week (Nov 9-13)

The number one movie on Prime Video this week is James Nunn’s 2026 creature feature Hungry. Starring Madison Davenport, the film follows a group of vacationers on a boat trip in Louisiana, where they encounter a deadly hippopotamus. While it’s had somewhat mixed reception from critics, it is a fun movie, but Hungry is hardly the only movie worth checking out on the streaming platform. Here’s a look at three great movies that we think you should watch on Prime Video this week.

For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Prime Video.

A film adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel directed by Mary Harron and starring Christian Bale, American Psycho is truly a 21st-century classic. The plot follows Bale’s Patrick Bateman, a wealthy New York City investment banker obsessed with his status, who leads a double life as a serial killer, hiding his psychopathic ego from his friends and acquaintances. The film also stars Willem Dafoe, Jared Leto, Justin Theroux, Chloë Sevigny, and Reese Witherspoon in notable roles.

Though initially considered an unfilmable novel, American Psycho has since become an icon of its genre, marked by Bale's disturbingly brilliant performance as the unhinged yuppie. The film can be called a darker mirror to 1987’s Wall Street, which blends psychological horror and black comedy to satirize the 1980s consumerist culture. When it first premiered in 2000, American Psycho received polarized reactions from critics and fans, receiving praise for the writing and acting, but also criticism for its gore and violence, though the latter has become significantly more appealing to audiences in subsequent years.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Based on the romance novel of the same name by Melissa Hill, Something from Tiffany’s is a holiday romance comedy directed by Daryl Wein. Starring Zoey Deutch as Rachel, the film sees her life suddenly upended when she mistakenly believes that her boyfriend, Gary, was going to propose to her, unaware that his real gift got switched, setting off a chain of serendipitous events. Kendrick Sampson, Ray Nicholson, and Shay Mitchell star as other key characters.

Something from Tiffany’s is a comforting, charming romcom that warms its way into your heart without needing any big moral or life lesson. The film has generally received a positive reception from critics and fans alike and has been praised for its lighthearted comedy and seasonal story. Something from Tiffany’s might not rank among the best Christmas romance movies of all time, but it surely does make the holiday movie experience cozier with its festive setting and adorable love story.

Actor-comedian Aziz Ansari’s feature directorial debut starring himself, Good Fortune follows Arj, a down-on-his-luck gig worker working for an uber-wealthy man named Jeff, whose life gets swapped with Jeff’s after an angel named Gabriel fails to show Arj the right path. This results in Gabriel losing his wings and living with mortals, while Arj and Jeff’s respective lives begin to unravel, leading to hilarious outcomes for all three of them. Keanu Reeves and Seth Rogen round out the main trio, with Keke Palmer and Sandra Oh as other notable characters.

Good Fortune is a strong directorial debut for Ansari, who brings his brand of humor alongside the phenomenal comedic deliveries of Reeves and Rogen, a combination that makes this film a delightful experience. While sometimes heavy-handed, the timely social satire and the comedic timing of the film are unmissable. The movie premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and has received generally favorable reviews from critics, earning praise for its quality humor and the comedic timing of its leading cast. The film easily ranks among the best comedies of 2025.

#3467. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3466. Report: iPad shipments drop 27.5% as global tablet market plunges in Q3

Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details.

According to a new report published by Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 11,5 million iPads during Q3 2026, accounting for 36% of all shipments.

Compared to Q3 2025, that was a 27.5% drop in shipments, and a 2.2 percentage-point decline in market share.

For context, the global tablet market saw a 23% year-over-year drop, with total shipments going from 41.8 million to 32.2 million units. Omdia noted this was the lowest level in nearly three years.

As for Apple’s competitors, Samsung remained in second place with 16.9% market share, followed by Lenovo with 12.7%, Xiaomi with 7.3%, and Huawei with 5.7%.

When it comes to shipment growth, Lenovo was the only company among the top five to post a positive result, up 11.9% year over year. Huawei saw the steepest decline at 43%, followed by Apple at 27.5%, Samsung at 21.7%, and Xiaomi at 10.6%.

Commenting on the results, Omdia Research Manager Himani Mukka said supply constraints are “limiting vendors’ ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors.”

“As a result,” she added, “consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

#3464. Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

“Hello, I’m Julie,” said a radiant Julianne Moore, holding out her hand as she popped out of the elevator at Middleburg, Virginia’s Salamander Resort. Her hair was red, her skin was white, her dress as yellow as gold. A few hours later after a rapturous Middleburg Film Festival reaction to “The Debut” (December 11), we talked in a hotel meeting room. The A24 crowdpleaser has been wowing audiences and critics since Telluride.

Jesse Eisenberg has done it again. His follow-up to “A Real Pain,” which won Kieran Culkin the Supporting Actor Oscar, could score Best Actress for Moore. The musical comedy has earned Moore raves on the festival circuit for her role as a sad suburban homemaker turned anxious aspiring actress in a New Jersey community theater. A sixth Oscar nomination is inevitable, and possibly a second Oscar win after “Still Alice” in 2015. It’s hard to believe she launched her career in 1988 as a regular on soap opera “As the World Turns.” Related Stories Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It? From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

Moore is the current Best Actress frontrunner, even though she has won before. Sometimes nabbing an Oscar is a disadvantage in the Oscar race. But not if the performance is undeniable: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four, while nipping at her heels are three-time winners Meryl Streep, Frances McDormand, Jack Nicholson, and Sean Penn.

Eisenberg wrote a rich character for Moore, knowing what the veteran actress could do with the childlike housewife Mona who, in order to learn how to act, must find herself. The director and actress had worked together on “When You Finish Saving the World” (2022). “[‘The Debut‘] is about this woman who has been chewed up but not spit out,” said Eisenberg, quoting Mona’s signature song. “It’s my point of view through somebody I consider a muse. I was writing something about myself as a seven-year-old in 1990, but I couldn’t picture anybody else except her doing it.”

It helped that Moore had told Eisenberg exactly what she was looking for. “I said I had just done ‘Dear Evan Hansen,’ and I loved singing, and I would love to have another opportunity,” she said. “I told him that I would love to do more comedy, and I didn’t want to play some suffering mom.”

Eisenberg put all of this in the screenplay, “but in the most surprising and inventive way,” she said. “He’s such a specific writer. He’s so incredibly empathetic. He has a compassionate worldview. He understands creativity. All of that stuff went into this wonderful and delightful story. It’s joyful and life-affirming too.”

Moore didn’t know she was playing a seven-year-old version of Eisenberg until he started telling that to the press. “Then he was like, ‘This is my experience of being a kid and going to community theater.’ But I could sense that there was a personal point of view in it. I very much felt with Mona that she was on a subjective journey, and that he was inside of that. With Mona, I always knew he was looking through her.”

“The Debut” is told from her point of view, as she tries to talk the overbearing local community theater director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) into hiring her, an untrained actress. He does it because he has no one else. But first, he must teach her how to act.

Mona dresses like a schoolgirl, with skirts, blouses, cardigan sweaters. “She’s so contained, and the way she learns is so literal,” said Moore, “the way a baby learns, like, you make a face at a baby, the baby makes a face back, but they don’t have intention behind it. But they’re learning things in an exterior way, and then they match it with feeling later on. So everything she’s doing is a childlike way of learning.”

Mona goes from an invisible nonentity in her own home to someone who demands attention. “She’s a kid who has found friends for the first time,” said Eisenberg. “She’s the girl who transferred to the right school at seven years old, and then the first rehearsal happens, and she is told she is terrible, and she has no idea why. And it’s the girl who transferred to the right school and gets an F on the very first test, and then the rest of the semester is panicking, and all she’s seeing is everybody else get A’s, and she still has the F, and she doesn’t know what to do. And then the teacher pulls her aside and says, ‘You either show up, or you are out on your ass.’ And something switches in her, and she makes the decision: ‘I am going to show up.’ And she begins to turn into a monster.”

The theater troupe embraces Mona as she unfolds like a flower. “We’ve been like those theater kids cracking corny jokes and finding community,” said Moore. “It’s all done with so much affection. Jesse looks at that world with not a hint of malice.”

Giamatti’s director relentlessly pushes the newbie through her paces until they have a powerful confrontation on the empty stage where he forces her to break down. Eisenberg reduced the actors’ anxiety by placing the eight-page showstopper in the middle of the shoot: not the beginning, and not the end. On the first day he went over to Moore’s apartment to talk about the movie. He said, “I really don’t want you to worry about that scene. I don’t want you to worry about memorizing that because I know that as an actor, I would I lose my mind. I would just be drilling it all the time, and I wouldn’t be able to concentrate. We’re going to have a teleprompter on that day. So don’t worry about it.”

So Moore worked on it normally, she said, “like I worked on everything else in the movie. So when we got to it, I knew it. I didn’t need a teleprompter. He knew instinctively as a director and an actor that what scares us sometimes is just a volume of language. He didn’t want to freeze me up. And having a partner like Paul who was so awake and aware and generous made it a pleasure. We were enjoying it when we did shoot it.”

Moore and Giamatti had never worked together before. She once introduced herself to him in a bookstore in Montauk. “He was very shy,” she said. “He is the greatest scene partner. I didn’t expect him to be so generous. He’s so funny, and he’s so dear. He’s present, incredibly modest, and as a partner, so available. Paul and I would work on it occasionally. When we were doing that scene, the rhythm was so important in it. You throw something, he hits it right back. It was our sense together of keeping it aloft, keeping it moving, keeping the river flowing. It felt electric with the two of us.”

The big blowout happens early in the story. “In a lot of movies, that kind of set piece would happen later,” said Moore. “Instead, it’s like a discovery place. It’s where she starts to begin to unlock herself emotionally, but she doesn’t learn from it. She comes in the next day, and starts to rehearse. And her belief is that acting is size, that it’s just huge, right? That’s when she starts yelling. She thinks it’s about being loud, which then allows her to go on the next journey with Jerry, where he says, ‘Let’s talk about feeling and reality and intention.’ So she’s slowly putting these pieces together. But that’s the first moment where she attaches something outside of herself to her own emotion.”

The whole shoot was fast, as Eisenberg didn’t have time to muck about and often shot just one take of a scene. “She and Paul Giamatti are so good on take one,” said Eisenberg. “It’s embarrassing. This is a small budget movie. The first two days of our schedule, we filmed in one day. The first two days, which were big ensemble musical numbers, we filmed in one day because we were prepared as a crew, but the actors were perfect on take one.”

Moore didn’t feel rushed. “It doesn’t feel, working with Jesse, like you’re moving too fast,” she said. “Working in independent film, you’re always moving quickly because you need to. You don’t have the time. You don’t have the money. So you want to move through things quickly. But I never felt rushed with him. I never I never felt like I was leaving something, that I didn’t get to complete something.”

The challenge for Moore, as it is for every actor shooting out of order, was making her character changes seamless. Eisenberg started with the theater scenes, then shot her family, and then jumped into Mona’s increasing weirdness. “The hardest thing always is making sure that you’ve pitched things correctly,” Moore said. “You want to make sure that you’ve managed to match it to another scene. So it was always hard to figure out. That’s our job.”

Eisenberg wanted Mona to move from looking quite childlike in the beginning, and swiftly move through her evolving transformations. Moore had fun with the costumes, figuring out the crazy wigs, makeup, and outfits in the second half. “Jesse had written that Mona electrocutes herself and destroys her hair, and that she was going to get her hair cut,” said Moore, “but he hadn’t written in a color change. We were messing around with it and trying to figure out what to do with hair and makeup and wardrobe and we had this idea that by having her dye her hair dark and chop it off, I wanted to homage the great ladies of musical theater, Liza Minnelli and Chita Rivera and Patti LuPone. It’s a wonderful Easter egg for that character.”

Making everything easier for Moore was actor-turned-director Eisenberg, who’d tell her when to ‘raise the stakes’ or ‘go hotter.’ “He’s maybe the most collaborative person I’ve ever worked with my entire life,” said Moore. “He listens to everyone. He asks people for opinions. He’ll ask people for notes, in a way that I would be like, ‘you don’t have to do that. This is your movie. It’s your creation.’ But he does collate opinion in a way. He’s fascinating in his generosity.”

Needless to say, singing her centerpiece song (“This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out”) was nervous-making, given that Moore was surrounded by Broadway super-belters like Tony winners Danny Burstein and Bonnie Tillman. “These people have the voices of angels,” said Moore. “When I did sing that song for the first time, and they’re all sitting there watching me, I think they did feel worried for me because they have so much ease. The song that she sings is so beautiful. In the singing of the song, she’s attaching her own emotional experience suddenly to the song. She understands the song in the moment she’s singing that. Somehow she wants more, and she knows that this is an avenue for her to find that. And so it’s a journey back to herself: finding that creativity and connection and community brings her to an essential sense of self.”

If degree of difficulty counts with Oscar voters, Moore may have that advantage.

#3463. The Dating Game's History After Rodney Alcala's Infamous Appearance

Lauren Garafano is a writer, editor, and digital media professional with a passion for pop culture, entertainment, beauty, and internet trends. She previously worked at BuzzFeed, creating content spanning celebrity news, television, and lifestyle, that garnered hundreds of thousands of views. She loves exploring the latest pop culture obsessions, beauty trends, and entertainment news to create engaging, relatable content that connects with readers.

With a background in digital journalism, Lauren specializes in features, news, reviews, explainers, listicles, SEO-driven content, and social media storytelling. She enjoys identifying emerging trends, crafting compelling headlines, and finding fresh angles on the topics audiences can’t stop talking about. Her experience also includes short-form video production, creative content development, and using audience analytics to inform editorial strategy.

Outside of writing, Lauren is passionate about theater and the performing arts, often spending her free time singing, dancing, performing, or working behind the scenes on community theater productions. She’s also an avid consumer of pop culture, beauty trends, and all things television, and she firmly believes there’s always another great story to uncover.

Netflix's hit movie Woman of the Hour, tells the horrifyingly true story of serial killer Rodney Alcala's appearance on the popular television game show The Dating Game. Directed by and starring Anna Kendrick, the film follows a woman named Sheryl Bradshaw, who appears as a contestant on the show. Unknown to Sheryl, the show's producers, and viewers, one of the potential suitors is Alcala (Daniel Zovatto).

While Woman of the Hour revolves around the horrifying story surrounding that one episode of the show, there's actually much more to The Dating Game's lore following Alcala's appearance. Despite having one of the most infamous contestants in TV history, the show continued to air for years after, even with several revivals decades later.

Alcala and Bradshaw appeared on The Dating Game back on September 13, 1978, and at the time nobody involved with the production knew he was a serial killer responsible for a number of murders happening in the '70s. Luckily, Bradshaw decided not to go on a date with him.

The Dating Game first premiered on ABC on December 20, 1965, and it quickly became one of the most popular game shows in the network's lineup. Created by television producer Chuck Barris, the premise of the game show featured contestants asking questions to three potential suitors before ultimately choosing one to go on a date with.

Shockingly, Alcala's appearance in 1978 didn't bring the show to an end, and it actually continued airing for two more years before its final episode in 1980. Since then, several revivals of the show have come about. Elaine Joyce hosted the 1986 revival and then Jeff MacGregor took over from 1987 to 1989.

The show later returned for another iteration in 1996. This time the show's format was updated to give contestants a chance to see their suitors before making their final decisions.

The most recent revival premiered in 2021, this time for a celebrity-themed edition of the show. This time around it was hosted by Zooey Deschanel and featured Michael Bolton as the musical co-host. However, it didn't last too long and ended after only eight episodes.

One detail that Woman of the Hour changes completely is the show's host. Tony Hale plays the fictional Ed Burke in the movie, but the actual host at the time was Jim Lange. Lange hosted the game show from its premiere in 1965 until 1980.

After his time on The Dating Game, Lange continued to work in television and radio, hosting other shows like Hollywood Connection and The New Newlywed Game. He worked in television broadcasting for decades before his death in 2014.

In an interview with CBR, Hale explained that the character of Ed Burke was created to represent the broader attitudes towards women at the time.

"He was kind of the symbol of how the culture was, treating women like how Sheryl was treated in her audition scene by the casting director. It wasn't just them. It was the acceptance of that and the allowance of that."

He also added that Burke's treatment of women created a different kind of trauma to contrast with the physical trauma inflicted by Alcala.

"But my character is causing trauma, because of how he's talking to these women, not listening to them, and treating them like objects. It's just sad."

Alcala became known as the "Dating Game Killer," but his crimes were not responsible for the show's eventual cancellation. He was convicted of multiple murders and sentenced to death in California, but both of his sentences were later overturned. He died in prison in 2021.

Alcala's full number of victims remains unknown. However, investigators have connected him to a series of murders and suspect his victim count could be over 130. His Dating Game appearance remains one of the spookiest things to happen in television history, especially because he was able to present himself as an ordinary, charming guy, despite his crimes.

While Woman of the Hour ends with Sheryl escaping Alcala, her real-life story provides some important context around this particularly dark episode. Bradshaw reportedly became uncomfortable after meeting Alcala in person and decided against going on a date with him — a decision which may have saved her life.

While Alcala's post-Dating Game story lives on, the other two contestants lived much quieter lives out of the spotlight. Their identities and what happened after the episode have not been publicly documented, though their presence is still important to the story.

#3461. WhatsApp’s AI-powered photo expansion tool starts rolling out on iOS

Select WhatsApp users on TestFlight and in the main app are now seeing the option to expand an image in the app’s photo editor. Here are the details.

iPhone users with access to Apple Intelligence have a native AI-powered photo expansion tool called Extend, which lets users pinch or drag to expand an image beyond its original borders.

This feature, which is also present on AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and image-editing platforms like Photoshop, is now also making its way into WhatsApp.

According to WABetaInfo, the platform is rolling out a Meta AI-powered image expansion tool, though it is currently limited to select users, primarily those in WhatsApp’s beta program via TestFlight.

When users select a photo in their chats, WhatsApp opens the drawing editor. Here, they can choose to apply some AI effect to improve it. Among these, users can find a new option to expand their photos. Once users select this option, Meta AI takes a few seconds to analyze the photo and generate the expanded version. Once the process is complete, WhatsApp shows the expanded photo in the drawing editor, and users can choose to send it. Note that this feature is also compatible with status updates.

The site notes that if the user isn’t happy with the result, they can tap an undo button to revert to the original and then try using the tool again to generate a different result.

As is usually the case with beta features on WhatsApp, there is no telling when it might become widely available.

That said, given that it has also rolled out to users in the Android beta and some users on the public iOS version already have access, a broader rollout might not be too far off.

#3460. 'Marshals' Cast Reveals the 'Yellowstone' Characters They Want Back the Most

A visit to the 'Marshals' set shows just how much work goes into producing CBS' major procedural series.

When Yellowstone ended, it felt like the Dutton family story was essentially over, especially for someone like Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes), who turned over a new leaf after selling his family's ranch back to the Broken Rock Tribe. He wrapped the series by finding peace with his wife, Monica (Kelsey Asbille), and son, Tate (Brecken Merrill) in East Camp. However, in Marshals, Kayce has been thrust back into the action. While Beth (Kelly Reilly) and Rip (Cole Hauser) have moved to Texas to build a new life, Kayce remains in Montana but now with a new role. As a U.S. marshal, Kayce has to face new threats, not only as a member of law enforcement, but also as a Dutton (with all of the baggage that comes with that name) and as a single father who has recently lost his wife.

Season 1 might have gotten off to a rocky start, especially due to the sharp format shift from Yellowstone's cable drama to Marshals' network TV procedural, but audiences still can't get enough of Taylor Sheridan's franchise. When Season 1 concluded with a cliffhanger ending, it felt inevitable that we would get more of Kayce's story. CBS renewed Marshals for 20 episodes for Season 2 (a step up from the 13-episode Season 1), giving the series more room to grow and develop its new cast of characters.

While Grimes and Merrill are reprising their roles, the show brings in some new faces with Logan Marshall Green as Pete "Cal" Calvin, the chief of the marshals team and Kayce's former U.S. Navy SEAL senior chief. There's also Belle Turek-Skinner (Arielle Kebbel), Andrea Cruz (Ash Santos), and Miles Kittel (Tatanka Means), who all work alongside Cal and Kayce week to week. From Broken Rock, both Gil Birmingham and Mo Brings Plenty return to play Thomas Rainwater and Mo, respectively. Despite its procedural format, Marshals still brings boatloads of action and thrills each week on CBS, and Collider had a chance to head to Park City, Utah, where the cast films the majority of the series to take a look at just what it takes to bring this Yellowstone spin-off to life.

Although both Yellowstone and Marshals technically take place in Montana, close to Bozeman, the majority of Marshals is filmed in Park City, Utah. At the Utah Film Studios, there are massive sets built in extreme detail. From the Marshals' headquarters office to Kayce's cabin to the Bullet 'n Barrel Saloon, each set is bursting at the seams with detail. There are news articles about Cal's past victories as a Navy SEAL on the walls, pictures of Monica and Tate in Kayce's cabin, and shotgun shell string lights decorating the rafters of the bar. The fireplace at the headquarters is made of real stone rather than foam, the beams of the bar and Kayce's cabin are made of real wood, and every inch of these sets is decorated and dressed with meticulous attention.

While the interiors are shot in a studio, the exteriors are shot around the area in Park City. One of the most significant locations seems to be Thousand Peaks Ranch, where Sheridan filmed his first few seasons of Yellowstone and Wind River. Locations like the historic Ontario Mine serve as the exterior to the marshals' headquarters, often filming on location when the team needs to head out of the office on a mission. On top of their typical filming locations, the production team also teased an upcoming train episode that is not only action-packed, but required that the production abide by federal regulations as they were filming on a real train.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

The costumes the characters wear are also looked at closely, with some of them carrying over from Yellowstone. Grimes still wears the same boots, jeans, belt, and hat as Kayce did in the original show. The hat, which comes from the Colorado shop Greeley Hat Works, is one of a kind. In a recent shoot that took Kayce to New York, the hat had to be handled with care during transportation, lest our cowboy U.S. marshal end up losing a key part of his look permanently. The costuming department sources the other cowboy hats from the local hat store in Park City called Warbonnet, while belt buckles specific to each character and their rodeo sports are made by retired Judge Leo Smith in Texas. If clothes need to be aged to look more worn in, the costuming department also has that down on lock, doing everything from spattering clothes with blood to tying a pair of boots to the back of a van so they can be banged up and aged to look weathered and worn.

Sitting down with the cast of Marshals — sans Marshall-Green, who just happened to be taking the day off — is a wild experience. Especially as the panel of stars takes seats at the Bullet 'n Barrell Saloon set, ready to dig into Season 2 of their CBS series. Alongside Grimes, Kebbel, Santos, Means, and Merrill is also Jefferson White, who is returning as Jimmy Hurdstrom from Yellowstone. For the large cast, the sophomore season is not only a boon but the increase of episodes is a sign of the network's faith in the show.

Santos, who immediately gets emotional, reveals that when she got the news about Season 2 from showrunner Spencer Hudnut, she sobbed in her car, calling the renewal a "tremendous win" and mentioning that the show helped her buy a house for herself. "I'll still cry about it today if I talk about it, because I just think it's amazing. It's wonderful," she says, her voice cracking a little. "The show changed my life overnight — financially, personally, and professionally. It's a huge gift, and it's not happening to everyone right now across our industry. There's a lot of actors who are unemployed, and a lot of crew members who are unemployed. So every day that I step on the set, I'm just grateful."

White, who is joining the show as a guest star, also notes that the higher episode count means more roles not only on the cast but in the crew. "It's a win for us personally, but it also makes me very proud and impressed with the work that these guys do to keep this show up and running, because there really is a trickle-down effect that affects everybody," White explains. "Because of this show, so many more people get their insurance, so many more people get their union hours." And despite a higher episode count meaning more work that might be ultimately more tiring, he calls the show "a win for the whole entertainment industry," saying, "I'm very proud to be a small part of it, and incredibly impressed by the Herculean effort that these guys do."

Of course, because Marshals exists in the same universe as Dutton Ranch, Santos is quick to mention Reilly as one of her ideal guest stars on the show, an idea that's not necessarily outside the realm of possibility considering both shows exist under the umbrella of Paramount. Less practical is Kebbel's desire to see Sam Elliott on their series. Elliott played Shea Brennan, a Pinkerton agent tasked with helping the Dutton family move west in 1883, and while there's no way his character could be in Marshals even if he had survived 1883, Kebbel still expresses wanting to see the iconic Western actor on the series.

Means mentions Tanaya Beatty who played Avery in Yellowstone, while Merrill gives a nod to Jen Landon's Teeter, and White wants to see Forrie J. Smith's Lloyd back to see how far Jimmy has come. For Grimes, the answer seems obvious and the one that has the largest potential of becoming a reality. "I'd like to see some flashbacks with Monica. She's the most important character to my character other than, you know, this one right here," he says, thumbing to Merrill seated next to him. "Obviously a lot happened that we didn't get to see, so I think those would be really hard scenes, because they wouldn't be the happiest, but I think it'd be great to just fill the audience in a little bit about how that all went out."

But although he is still mourning his wife, that doesn't mean that romance is completely out of the question, as Marshals is very clearly setting up a relationship between Kayce and Andrea. Grimes admits that he and Hudnut both knew that there would have to be a romantic interest for Kayce. But Grimes had a caveat. "I was like, it's gotta take a long time, because let's give Kayce and the audience some time to deal with Monica's passing, and let's really honor that and respect that," Grimes explains. While it seemed obvious to them that his love interest would ideally be someone on the marshals team, Grimes isn't interested in rushing into things. Comparing Kayce and Andrea to The Office's Jim and Pam, he calls the relationship a "real nice old-school slow play," jokingly adding, "Let's just really try and act like it's not going to happen for a while. That's been in the plans before there ever was a first script."

For Birmingham, who is returning to the role of Thomas Rainwater, the new series operates at a much faster pace. "You don't have the time allotment to really play the characters out as much because the format is different." But the show does offer a chance to explore the internal dynamics of the reservation more as Season 2 digs into the conflict between the people of Broken Rock and their opposition to Rainwater's leadership.

"I've had conversations with Spencer, talking about storylines in that regard, how closely do these follow the culture itself, relationships, and how the tribe behaves toward the chairman, and the responsibilities the chairman has," Birmingham explains. "I think that's the biggest lesson I've learned is how heavy that load is. He's responsible for the welfare — psychologically, spiritually, economically — and then you're getting monetary influxes that are necessary to sustain, but cross a moral ambiguity, and makes it tough."

It turns out that Kayce can't fully forget his past, after all.

The franchise has always been very conscious of the way it mingles the Duttons with the Native Americans of Broken Rock. Birmingham points out that when Sheridan was younger, he found clarity after sitting in a sweat lodge. "He was on a personal spiritual journey of his own. He was younger, and nothing really resonated for him until he did a sweat. And then the man who directed that sweat was saying, 'Well, if you are apprehensive about this, let me refer you over to the Lakota people, and he got introduced to some elders there," Birmingham explains.

"He lived over there for several years, and that's where some of his stories come out of. He's heard them, hundreds of them. Wind River spin out of that. So he has a real understanding of the culture." However, Birmingham notes that Marshals faces challenges because Sheridan is not as closely involved. "We're relied upon for collaborating, Mo [Brings Plenty], and I, Tatanka, with the native culture element. It's just a learning curve," he says, "because if you're not immersed in it, if you're not familiar with it, then you won't really know how to depict these characters or their relationships."

Marshals also offers the opportunity for someone like Mo Brings Plenty to expand on his character a bit more, and Birmingham refers to him as a cultural anchor for the series, saying, "I don't think Taylor was aware that Mo's an elder in the Lakota nation," and that Brings Plenty's experience as a cowboy Indian will bring aspects of the culture that aren't often portrayed in television. For Brings Plenty, the opportunity to expand his character also allows the show to explore more Native American storylines.

One personal story to Brings Plenty ties back to his recently deceased nephew, Cole Brings Plenty, who was reported missing in March 2024 and then found dead in a wooded area in Kansas a month later. For Brings Plenty, having a storyline on Marshals that reflects the frustration and struggle his family has had trying to figure out the truth of what happened to his nephew is pivotal. "It's a storyline that has impacted our family very much, and we're not the only family in this country that has experienced this situation," he explains, referencing the upcoming Episode 6 "Roughstock" that will focus in on Mo bringing in Kayce to help investigate his missing nephew.

"I can't wait for it to come out," Brings Plenty says. "I'm hopeful that it'll evolve into something that will spark an interest in this country, to get more people in society involved and care about what's occurring to American Indian peoples throughout this country." Although Brings Plenty acknowledges that it won't bring his nephew back, the impact of the story could make a difference for the other young people in America.

"If we don't start making noise about it or speaking to our senators or Congresspeople, then it's something that will continue: the lawlessness. Because the wheels of justice don't really turn for us as American Indian people, we have to get involved. It's something that's near and dear to my heart." For Brings Plenty, the opportunity to highlight his culture and show more than just the stereotypical depiction of Native Americans is something he can be grateful to CBS for. "I'm thankful because a lot of networks wouldn't take that chance. They wouldn't be supportive of that," he explains, pointing out that just seeing this representation at work means that "the good outlasts the bad."

#3459. King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution

“Godzilla Minus Zero” builds on the strong visual foundation — and/or the rubble of Tokyo’s Ginza district — that director Takashi Yamazaki pounded into his previous film, “Godzilla Minus One.” Like that first film, “Minus Zero” is in conversation with the big ideas and cultural/emotional resonances behind Toho’s giant monsters, and it’s attuned to the beloved visual details of the franchise, going all the way back to the original “Godzilla” and the Shōwa era.

But historically, for all kinds of budgetary and technological reasons, King Ghidorah is usually not ready for his close-up.

The amount of time that “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends with its three-headed mutant space dragon on the ground is a notable departure from how Ghidorah is most often depicted: in flight, or towering far above Godzilla. Even in closer shots in a CGI-rich film like “Godzilla: King of the Monsters,” when all three heads get ready to chomp up a puny human or 10, the emphasis is on Ghidorah’s scale. Three heads are more terrifying than one. Related Stories Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It? From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

But “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends a lot of time with just one head, or focused on just one head, and its Ghidorah is as scary on the ground as it is in the air, and this is in part due to the particular design experience that director Yamazaki and his team brought to the world’s deadliest gold dragon. Yamazaki was tapped to design “Godzilla the Ride” at Seibuen Amusement Park (its full name is Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle) in 2021 and therefore had to figure out a version of Ghidorah that would work from the other side of a safety rail.

Yamazaki and animation studio Shirogumi worked on a monster concept that would feel, according to “Minus One” and “Minus Zero” producer Kazuaki Kishida, “as though the audience was under attack by Ghidorah itself. So it had to be very scary and very close-up,” Kishida told IndieWire. “[In the ride,] we see Ghidorah basically crawling on the ground with its neck, because it has a very long neck, and then really going after the audience. To bring King Ghidorah very close to humans and bring the eyeline closer was a huge core concept for this. So there was a lot of research that had gone into the ride that we were able to apply to ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.'”

The film uses Ghidorah’s eyeline to great effect. One of the most unnerving moments in its initial attack on Matsumoto City, as scientists Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) and Akira Hagiwara (Ko Maehara) scramble to both document the new monster on the block and survive the utter destruction of whole city blocks, is a moment of getting really, uncomfortably close to Ghidorah’s eye.

That forced proximity to Ghidorah makes all the spectacular space-dragon stuff it can do even more effective, though these effects are also as grounded in the natural and the tangible as much as possible. For Ghidorah’s destructive beam, for instance, visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima did more research than even he thought he could do on how lightning visualizes itself.

“Everyone sort of recognized the string of light, that line of light. But if you look at lightning in slow motion, it leaves a line of something that lingers — this is apparently just water vaporizing instantly and turning into plasma,” Nojima told IndieWire. “I don’t fully know the science behind it, but there’s a visual effect that lightning leaves behind. So for Ghidorah’s destruction beam, I wanted to emphasize that element of it. I scatter particles around, kind of blur the imagery, and then let it linger longer than it normally would.”

Of course, whenever the destruction beam hits something, Nojima and the VFX team got to build the explosion. But it’s that visual sense of Ghidorah’s power lingering, and of getting too close to where Ghidorah can see you, that makes this version of the monster feel so dangerous.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3458. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3457. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3456. Netflix's 4-Season Dark Fantasy Series Was This Close To Greatness

Netflix really had something great on its hands with its four-season dark fantasy series, but it fell short in the very last moments. The world of television is already pretty unforgiving, and the streaming landscape has made it even harder for projects to stand out amid a sea of content. The fantasy genre doesn't make things any easier, since it's all too common for these shows to flop after only a single season if they don't check all the right boxes. It's for all these reasons that it's rather remarkable when anything sticks.

One of these remarkable TV shows is Netflix's The Umbrella Academy. The show premiered in 2019 and pretty quickly proved itself to be unlike any other fantasy series on screens. The Umbrella Academy is deliciously dark, but this is layered up with a quirky, character-driven narrative that aims to subvert the superhero genre at every turn. This isn't an ordinary Marvel or MCU show. Instead, Umbrella Academy is all about complicated families.

The story of The Umbrella Academy revolves around a group of seven adopted children with miraculous abilities who are raised as a superhero team, known, of course, as the Umbrella Academy. This family ultimately fractured and dissolved, but the estranged siblings find their reunion as adults following their adoptive father's death. The show is all time travel and apocalypse-level events, layered with family dysfunction and character quirks. For its first three seasons, The Umbrella Academy was on top of the world. Unfortunately, season 4 is when things collapsed.

It's important to note that, otherwise, The Umbrella Academy is an excellent series that is still entirely worth watching. Unfortunately, there is really no denying that the fourth and final season really missed the mark. While seasons 2 and 3 both earned impressive 91% scores on Rotten Tomatoes, season 4 came in shockingly low at a "rotten" 55%. Something went wrong, and critics had no trouble pointing out exactly what.

First things first, The Umbrella Academy season 4 suffered because of its rushed narrative. While previous installments were made up of 10 episodes, season 4 had only six. It simply wasn't enough time to meaningfully wrap up the established story, but things got even worse when the episodes seemed to focus on all the wrong things. Beloved characters were misused or abandoned, tired plot devices were repeated, and the final big twist of Umbrella Academy felt, to many, like a slap to the face. Overall, it was just unfortunate.

The fact that, despite all of this, The Umbrella Academy is still an easy show to recommend is really a testament to the excellence of those first few seasons, especially seasons 2 and 3. It is perhaps better to know ahead of time that the ending won't satisfy the way many would have hoped. However, if you hope to give this fantasy series a try, keep in mind that the ending may still be revised.

Like many great superhero TV shows, The Umbrella Academy is based on a comic book series. Like many other great fantasy TV shows, The Umbrella Academy got ahead of its source material. This meant that Netflix's writers were on their own for season 4 and its ending, on top of the disadvantage of having to wrap things up in six episodes. The good news is that future installments of The Umbrella Academy are on the way, with original creators Gerard Way and Gabriel Bá continuing to put out new content.

Since The Umbrella Academy came to its unfortunate close in 2024, the comics have proceeded with several new issues, the most recent having been released on October 28, 2026. The series finale, issue #6, is expected to hit shelves near the beginning of 2027. This will definitively wrap up the story as it was intended to be, and there will be absolutely no need to rush through in the way Netflix did. So, if you get hooked on The Umbrella Academy, take comfort in the knowledge that there is still light at the end of the tunnel.

#3455. Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo

While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.

As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”

He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”

The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:

The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo

Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.

The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.

For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.

To read Apple’s full support article, follow this link. And make sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the new MacBook Pro.
